findings.location: ## 2. Official Data Feeds: DHM, BIPAD and NEMRC (intro paragraph and ### B / ### D)
findings.issue: NEMRC is one of the three data sources the query names, and the decomposition requires 'what is available, reliability, how to use better' for it. The draft never covers it properly. It appears only as 'locates earthquakes', as one item in a list of slow products ('NEMRC's catalogue'), and as 'NEMRC events linked to USGS' (M7). Nothing says what NEMRC publishes, what format it uses, how its magnitudes relate to USGS/EMSC values, or what reliability problems the scrape has. The corpus has no NEMRC-specific source. The only evidence is the repo inspection in interim-report-atlas-role-in-warning-ecosystem: NEMRC is an HTML scrape, not verified, and may need JS rendering. The draft does not say that this gap exists.
findings.evidence: temp/interim-report-atlas-role-in-warning-ecosystem.md line 8: 'DHM bulletins, forecast, NEMRC and NDRRMA are HTML scrapes, three need JS rendering, none verified.' The coverage-matrix marks the 'daily copy of official DHM/BIPAD/NEMRC data' row OK, but no vault note covers NEMRC outputs. A vault search for 'NEMRC' returns only the interim report.
findings.recommendation: In section 2 (intro or B), add two or three sentences on NEMRC. The NEMRC copy is an unverified HTML scrape. Its records should carry the agency's own magnitude type and timestamp (Nepal time) and be shown beside USGS/EMSC values for the same event, with a note that early magnitudes get revised. Flag that the research found no documentation of a machine-readable NEMRC feed or of its revision practice. Make it a validation item, for example adding a NEMRC-versus-USGS catalogue match rate to the V4 feed-health audit. Do not invent NEMRC facts.

findings.location: ## 3. The Map and Place Search, ### A. Search is a language problem (and table row N6 / M12)
findings.issue: The query names 'Nepali district names from the constitution', and the decomposition asks for its 'extension to other admin levels/places'. The draft keeps constitutional names 'authoritative for districts' and fills the 753 local levels and wards from OSM, with a rule never to present OSM names as official. It does not ask whether provinces and local levels have an official Nepali name source the project should adopt the same way. It also does not mention the Survey Department transliteration standard as the authority for romanised spellings. That standard is in the corpus, and the draft cites it only as an OSM community resolution. So the draft never answers the extension question directly.
findings.evidence: nepalmeetings2022-12-15-openstreetmap-wiki ([33]): OSM Nepal resolved to follow the Survey Department's transliteration standard. keynamene-openstreetmap-wiki ([34]). government-invites-feedback-on-disability-law-online-but-target-group-is-locked (uncited): 2021 Directive on government websites requires Unicode and Nepali+English. prompt-decomposition.json entity 'Nepali district names from the constitution' has required_fields ['extension to other admin levels/places'].
findings.recommendation: Add a short paragraph to 3A covering three points. First, extend the constitutional-name approach upward to the 7 provinces and downward to the 753 local levels, using the official government list of local-level names (Nepali plus official romanisation) as the authoritative layer, with OSM name:ne/alt_name used only as search aliases. Second, adopt the Survey Department transliteration standard for any English spelling the Atlas itself generates. Third, mark each name's source tier (constitutional, official list, OSM) in the place panel. Note that the corpus did not retrieve the official local-level name list itself, so this is a recommendation still to be checked, not a verified data source.

findings.location: ## 4. Flood and Glacial-Lake Outburst Scenarios, ### C (source size) and ### D (origins)
findings.issue: The corpus has a cluster of EGU abstracts on GLOF data that the draft omits. (1) A Himalaya-wide mapping of past GLOFs adds more than 200 new events to the 108 already compiled. It finds that GLOF frequency from moraine-dammed lakes over the last 20 years is markedly lower than in 1970–2000, even though lakes have grown. This bears on a historical-GLOF layer and on how the Atlas frames climate trends. (2) A bathymetry study finds that the volume–area empirical relations used for unsurveyed lakes show 'substantial discrepancies' against measured volumes. That directly supports the draft's 'uncertain by a factor of several' label for Tier 3 volumes, but the draft gives the label no source. (3) The 2023 South Lhonak (Sikkim) GLOF had transboundary effects 'hundreds of kilometers' downstream and destroyed the Teesta III hydropower project 63 km below the lake. It is a regional precedent for the cascade branch and for hydropower exposure.
findings.evidence: abstract-egu23-15703 (McCoy et al., EGU23): '>200 newly mapped GLOFs from ~200 lakes ... GLOF frequency from moraine-dammed lakes in the last 20 years is markedly lower than earlier time periods'. abstract-egu25-14977: 'volume-area empirical relations ... have shown substantial discrepancies'. abstract-egu25-768 (Sattar, Cook et al.): South Lhonak 2023, 'transboundary effects extending hundreds of kilometers', Teesta III destroyed 63 km downstream. None of the three is cited.
findings.recommendation: In 4C, add one sentence citing EGU25-14977 as the reason area-based volume estimates carry a wide range. In 4D or 8C, add one or two sentences on a 'past outbursts' reference layer built from published GLOF compilations, with the caveat that the recent mapped frequency is lower and that mapping bias undercounts older events. The Atlas should present lake growth as change in exposure, not as rising outburst frequency. In 4B, add South Lhonak 2023 as a regional example of a destructive far-field cascade with infrastructure losses. Grade all of these C (abstracts).

findings.location: ## 2. Official Data Feeds, ### A or ### C (DHM river stations)
findings.issue: Several DHM-specific corpus notes are unused, so the draft says little about what DHM data actually is. DHM's hydrometric network reports water level (stage), not real-time discharge, from about 150 stations for 6,000+ rivers. Telemetry runs at 5-minute intervals in the monsoon. Large-river forecasts use MIKE 11, and mass SMS uses polygon targeting (13 million SMS in 2079 BS). For the Atlas, the key fact is that the scenario engine reports peaks in m³/s while DHM gauges report stage against warning levels. The draft's two-branch peak display and 'nearest gauge' place panel can therefore not be compared directly with live gauge values, and the draft does not warn about this mismatch.
findings.evidence: nepal-wants-to-power-south-asia-it-does-not-know-what-its-rivers-are-doing: '~150 hydrometric stations for 6,000+ rivers, level only, no real-time discharge' (opinion, grade C). some-recent-developments-in-hydro-meteorological-data: DHM 5-minute monsoon telemetry over CDMA/GPRS. early-warning-system-and (DHM NCDRR 2023 presentation): MIKE 11 on large rivers, polygon-targeted mass SMS, 13 million SMS. None is cited.
findings.recommendation: Add two or three sentences to 2A or 2C. DHM's network is sparse and stage-based, telemetered every few minutes in monsoon, with model-based forecasts only on large rivers. As a result, the Atlas's place panels should show gauge stage against DHM's own warning level and should not convert stage to discharge or compare it with scenario peaks in m³/s. Also note that the daily copy throws away most of a 5-minute signal, which supports the archive and data-age points already made.

findings.location: ## 6. Serving Nepali Users, ### C or ### D
findings.issue: Nepal's 2021 Directive on government websites (Unicode, adjustable fonts, responsive design, Nepali+English) is an official national benchmark the Atlas could state it meets. The corpus also documents that government content in Preeti or as image files locks out screen-reader users. The draft cites Prayatna and WCAG but not this national rule, which would give the accessibility work local legitimacy with agency partners.
findings.evidence: government-invites-feedback-on-disability-law-online-but-target-group-is-locked (Kathmandu Post, Apr 2026): draft disability law published as images and in Preeti, unreadable to screen readers. The 2021 Directive on government websites requires Unicode, adjustable fonts, responsive design and Nepali+English, but enforcement is weak. Not cited.
findings.recommendation: In 6C or 6D, add one sentence saying the Atlas should state that it meets Nepal's 2021 government-website directive as well as WCAG, citing the Kathmandu Post piece. Add a second sentence noting that even the government's own disability-law consultation failed this test, which shows why the Atlas's Unicode and accessible-print rules matter.

findings.location: ## 5. Earthquake Scenarios, ### E. What earthquake scenarios are for
findings.issue: The draft treats the GEM/BGS METEOR grid as a long-term reference. It omits the corpus point that Nepal's national seismic hazard map is about two decades old, and that an OpenQuake-based national risk study exists with a 1934-recurrence damage and loss scenario. That matters for the 1934 historical preset and explains why an open probabilistic grid is worth showing.
findings.evidence: seismic-risk-assessment-and-hazard-mapping-in-nepal (Chaulagain et al. 2015, Nat Hazards 78:583–602, abstract only): OpenQuake national hazard and loss maps at 1/2/5/10% PoE in 50 years, plus building damage and loss for a recurrence of the 1934 earthquake, noting the national hazard map is ~2 decades old. Not cited.
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence to 5E. The official national hazard map dates from the 1990s, and published OpenQuake studies, including a 1934-recurrence scenario, give the Atlas's 1934 preset a published comparison, in the same way the Gorkha preset gets a hindcast. Grade C (abstract).

findings.location: ## 8. Missing Hazards and Capabilities, ### C (impact information)
findings.issue: The corpus has concrete impact figures from 2024 and 2026 that would make the recommendation to count OSM schools, health posts, bridges and hydropower intakes more concrete, but the draft does not use them. After the 2026 event, about 748 MW of hydropower and more than 30 bridges were affected. FAO's DIEM-Impact assessment of the September 2024 floods recorded 71 municipalities in 20 districts declared crisis zones. The municipality-level framing supports the ward/municipality summaries the draft recommends.
findings.evidence: irdr-addressing-the-challenges-of-natural-human-induced-environmental-hazards (IRDR rapid report, 28 Aug 2026): ~748 MW hydropower affected, >30 bridges. nepal-flood-impact-assessment (FAO DIEM-Impact, doi 10.4060/cd5014en): 71 municipalities across 20 districts declared crisis/emergency zones in Sept 2024. Neither is cited.
findings.recommendation: In 8C, add one sentence using the IRDR figures to show that hydropower and bridges carry much of the infrastructure loss in outburst and cascade events, which justifies including them in footprint counts. Optionally, add the FAO municipality count to support municipality-level summaries.

findings.location: ## 2. Official Data Feeds, ### C. Agency warning levels, and CAP consumed but not emitted
findings.issue: The draft recommends a CAP reader 'on the day a feed appears' but does not say where that feed would be found. The corpus covers WMO's Severe Weather Information Centre 3.0 and the Register of Alerting Authorities, which is how WMO members' official CAP feeds are listed and aggregated. That gives the CAP reader a concrete discovery path. It also supports the 'never emit CAP' argument, because only registered alerting authorities are aggregated. GSMA's finding that Nepal's SMS alerts are manual and prone to congestion and delay is also unused.
findings.evidence: severe-weather-information-centre-30: SWIC 3.0 aggregates CAP warnings from WMO Members and links to the Register of Alerting Authorities and a CAP checker. mobile-enabled-anticipatory-action-and-early-warning-systems-the-gsma-and-fcdo-v: Nepal's location-based SMS is manual and congestion/delay prone; cell broadcast under discussion with NDRRMA/DHM. Neither is cited.
findings.recommendation: In 2C, add one sentence. The CAP reader should watch the WMO Register of Alerting Authorities and SWIC for a Nepal entry, and validate any feed it finds with WMO's CAP checker. The register lists only official authorities, which is a further reason the Atlas should not publish its own CAP feed. Optionally, cite the GSMA blog in 8D for the claim that SMS is manual and delay-prone.

findings.location: Whole draft (about 69 KB); especially §2A closing paragraph, §8D, §9A, §10D, §10E
findings.issue: Content dilution. The report is about 69 KB, above the 45–55 KB range of top performers. The thesis that the Atlas 'complements and does not compete with the official warning chain' is restated almost in full at least five times: end of §2A ('should supply that content in advance, not compete with the warning chain'), §2C (no own CAP feed), §8D ('would turn a complement into a competing authority'), §9A, §10D ('Do not run a warning channel...'), and §10E ('misread as a competing authority'). The 'errors lean toward reassurance' thesis is also repeated in the executive summary, §1B and §1C. §10E 'Looking ahead' largely re-lists CAP, cell broadcast, BIPAD impact-based forecasting, open inventories and EW4All, all of which were already covered in §§2, 8 and 9.
findings.recommendation: Make three cuts. (1) Merge §8D into §10D, which already lists the same 'do not build' items, and keep only the cell-broadcast citation. (2) Cut §10E by about half: keep the Betrawati 'how long do I have here' passage and drop the re-list of CAP, cell broadcast, BIPAD and EW4All already covered. (3) Cut the restatement of the 'complement, not competitor' line at the end of §9A to one clause. Doing this would free about 3–5 KB, enough to absorb the coverage additions above without growing the report.
